newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan ministries fight over Euroyen tax plan.
newsitem.headline: Japan ministries fight over Euroyen tax plan.

text.p: Japan's trade ministry is fighting hard to block a finance ministry plan to scrap exemptions on a withholding tax on income from Euroyen bond investments by foreigners, sources at both ministries said on Tuesday.
The Ministry of International Trade and Industries (MITI) said it was supporting Japanese firms who want the exemptions kept.
"There have been strong requests from various domestic industries to keep the law," a MITI official said.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) says it want to repeal the law to close a loophole which allows the tax break on Euroyen purchases by Japanese investors who buy the bonds through overseas subsidiaries of Japanese firms.
"We will assist the firms as much as possible to fulfil their needs. There is a need to secure this law so they can raise funds as smoothly as possible," the MITI official said.

MITI and a group of leading domestic firms have urged the Finance Ministry to keep the exemption, saying Euroyen bonds were one of the most effective fund-raising tools, and a much more efficient way to raise funds than domestic bonds.
They said the firms would face difficulties raising funds if the exemption was scrapped.

"I'm getting an impression the MOF is very narrow-minded. It seems the MOF is seeing things from a taxation point of view, but ignoring the effect it will have on the Euroyen market," said a senior official at a major trading firm.
"Many domestic firms could face difficulties raising funds through the Euro market. There is also a danger the Euroyen market could shrink," the trading firm official said.

In early October, more than 50 leading Japanese firms, including giants like Nippon Steel Corp, Toyota Motor , Tokyo Gas , Hitachi Ltd and Tokyo Electric Power Co , issued a statement opposing the MOF's plan.
Industry sources said there were signs opposition to the plan was growing in several industry groups.
But MOF has resisted the firms, saying it mainly needs to scrap the law because non-Japanese residents are not buying the Euroyen bonds.
MOF said the tax rule was originally intended to stimulate Euroyen purchases by non-Japanese residents, but Japanese investors have become the main buyers.
MOF said it wants to do away with the law so it can close the tax loophole used by investors who buy the bonds through overseas subsidiaries of Japanese firms.
"We still don't see the need to keep the law. There is no convincing fact to keep it," a MOF official said. "The law was originally for the use for non-Japanese residents.

"We've asking them (MITI and the firms) to provide us with data that shows non-Japanese residents are the main buyers of the Euroyen (bonds). We need to see reasonable facts to justify their point...but so far we received nothing," he said.
MOF intends to abolish the tax exemption rule by April 1998, when it was also expected to abolish the current 40-day lock-up rule on domestic sales of Euroyen bonds issued by Japanese borrowers.
MOF and MITI officials said they were likely to meet sometime this week.
